cards.title: TikTok Shop product screening criteria (Baseline)
cards.summary: A seven-point filter for screening TikTok Shop products for dropshipping tests, including renewable potential, problem-solving angle, ad age, revenue trend and range, and English-speaking market.
cards.use_when: Screening a raw list of TikTok Shop products in a research tool (Kalodata/Shop Plus) before committing budget to a test.
steps: Check if the product is renewable — can you build a subscription or repeat-purchase offer around it? This is optional, not a dealbreaker, but the source prioritizes it because it enables long-term brand building and recurring revenue.

Confirm it solves a real problem or insecurity. The source claims many beginner picks fail because the perceived problem is too small; winning products often converge on the same desires (anti-bloat, slimming, energy, looking/feeling better) with different marketing angles and ingredients.
Verify the ad creatives are new to the market, not just that revenue exists. Look at the videos actually promoting the product, not only the revenue figure.
Require a strong upward revenue trend, not a flat or declining one.
Keep revenue moderate: the source's target is roughly $33K–$97K in the last 30 days. Products doing $300K–$1M+/month signal heavy competition rather than opportunity.
Prefer English-speaking products; the source discards products whose ads are entirely in Spanish because they succeed by selling to Latin American buyers, not the US market.
Treat this as a blueprint, not a hard rulebook — the source explicitly warns beginners against turning criteria into a 'bible' and says conviction can justify breaking filters.
caveats: The revenue range and thresholds are the source's personal working numbers, not validated benchmarks.
The criteria are explicitly described as flexible; strict adherence can cause missed winners.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Reading 30-day vs 180-day revenue graphs in Kalodata
cards.summary: How to use the 30-day graph to spot uptrends, then immediately switch to 180-day data to reject products that peaked months ago.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product's visible growth in the default research-tool view is real momentum or a dying product that only looks alive in a short window.
steps: In the product list, ignore the product images on first pass — the source covers them with a hand and looks only at the graph shape. Look for a graph that is flat or tilting upward, not one pointing to the sky.
Click a product whose 30-day graph looks slightly upward, then immediately switch to the 180-day view to get the full picture.
In the 180-day view, reject the product if it was selling months ago and is now flatlining near the bottom — e.g. previously hitting highs of ~1K/day and now doing roughly one sale per day.
Watch for the pattern where a product dipped and is now climbing back up; the source finds this interesting enough to investigate further, whereas a straight downtrend is an immediate skip.
Treat a product only recently launched with a steeply rising 180-day curve (e.g. 2K → 16K → 21K → 20K over successive periods) as a strong green flag for early entry.
caveats: Switching back to the 180-day view can completely reverse a 30-day impression; the source calls this 'getting the full picture' and says it prevents wasted testing spend.
Products on a straight vertical graph have no downside data, so sustainability is unknown — the source calls these 'gamble products'.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Video age and revenue distribution checks
cards.summary: Validate a product by requiring a top-performing video posted in the last 7–14 days and revenue spread across at least three to five recent videos rather than one old hero video.
cards.use_when: After a product passes the revenue-graph screen, before deciding whether you have enough proven creative to build an ad test.
steps: Open the product's video tab and check the posting dates of the top-performing videos. The highest-revenue video must have been posted within the last 7 to 14 days.
Reject products where an old video (months old) is still carrying revenue — an old ad running with an ad symbol can indicate a brand trying to revive a dead product rather than fresh momentum.
Check revenue distribution across the top videos. Discard products where 90%+ of revenue comes from a single old video.
Require at least 3–5 recent videos contributing meaningful revenue so you have multiple proven creatives to work with.

Use the 7-day view in addition to the 180-day view: the top ad in the recent window can differ from the top ad historically, and the most recent proven creative is the one most likely to transfer to your own Meta test.

Exception the source allows: if the product's recent revenue is large enough (e.g. ~60K in 7 days), a top video with 58K versus a second video at 600 is acceptable, because conviction from overall validation outweighs the distribution rule — you can pair the winning hook with other weaker clips.
caveats: A single dominant creative means you lack proven assets for your own campaign, raising execution risk even if the product concept is strong.
The source's own exception (high recent revenue justifies a lopsided distribution) is a judgment call, not a rule.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Filtering out live-sales and cheap-impulse products
cards.summary: Reject TikTok Shop products whose revenue comes primarily from live streams or whose price point depends on cheap impulse buying.
cards.use_when: Screening candidate products in Kalodata and interpreting price and revenue-source data.
steps: Check the revenue source breakdown. The source sets 'video' as the required revenue source, because it wants video/UGC creatives, not live-stream sales.
Get off the product immediately if live revenue is around 25K or higher — that indicates success driven by live streams rather than transferable video ads.
Reject products selling at roughly $9.99. The source treats this as a major red flag because cheap impulse buys rarely carry enough margin to survive Meta acquisition costs.
Apply these as filters alongside the graph checks, not in isolation — a strong graph with a cheap price is still a skip.
caveats: Live-commerce can be a legitimate channel in other contexts; this filter is specific to dropshippers whose model depends on video ads and Meta traffic.
The 25K live-revenue threshold and $9.99 rejection are the source's heuristics, not measured breakpoints.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Using revenue filters and the law of diminishing returns
cards.summary: How to set and adjust the revenue range filter based on whether previous tests produced profitable or unprofitable sales.
cards.use_when: Setting the revenue range in Kalodata and iterating on it after a test result.
steps: The source treats the revenue range as a lenient, changeable filter — the specific numbers used (e.g. 55K–97K) were chosen arbitrarily, and the source says any nearby value would work the same.

Evaluate results before adjusting: if a product did a lot of sales but was highly unprofitable and had been doing ~20K/month in revenue, raise the range on the next hunt (e.g. to 40K) and test again to see if profitability improves.
Be aware of diminishing returns: pushing the range to 200K–300K brings you into the most competitive space, which is 'playing with fire' rather than a shortcut to profitability.
Remember the source's rationale: TikTok Shop customer demand translates over to Meta, so TikTok revenue level is usable as a proxy for market demand when setting the filter.
Set revenue source to 'video' and avoid using the 'growing' trend filter — the source says selecting it makes Kalodata hide many good products.
caveats: The relationship between higher TikTok revenue and Meta profitability is not guaranteed; the source frames it as something to test empirically.
Very high revenue products come with heavy competition, not just validation.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Validating a sub-niche trend on Google Trends
cards.summary: Validate that the exact product variation — not the broad category — has an active 12-month upward trajectory on Google Trends.
cards.use_when: After a specific product passes tool screening and you want trend confirmation before testing, especially for emerging formats like patches.
steps: Search the exact variation, not the parent keyword. Example: search 'GLP-1 patches' rather than just 'GLP-1'.
Check the 12-month graph. It must show an active, current upward trajectory — not a peak that has already flattened.

Use the comparison insightfully: in the source's example, the broad 'GLP-1' term was at an all-time high (index 100, rare on Google Trends) while the 'GLP-1 patches' variation was on its own rising uptrend — indicating an early sub-niche with room to grow.
Treat this step as optional. The source skips it when conviction is already high and goes straight to testing, calling the Google Trends check a sidetrack when he is convinced.
caveats: The source explicitly marks this step optional and says it can slow down execution.
Google Trends measures search interest, not purchase intent.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Competition assessment via Facebook Ad Library and Page Transparency
cards.summary: Assess how many direct competitors are running the product, how long they've been running, and whether their stores and offers look beatable.
cards.use_when: Validating saturation and competitive positioning right before you decide to buy or build the store.
steps: Search the product term in Facebook Ad Library. Assess the whole niche first (e.g. all GLP products: gummies, liquids, pills, powders), then narrow to your exact variation (e.g. GLP patches).
Open the page for each competitor, go to About → Page Transparency, confirm whether the page is currently running ads, then open their ad library to see every active ad.

Note how long they have been running. A competitor running ads for only nine hours has no spend history, so their ads validate nothing yet — the source says to bookmark them and watch rather than infer a winner.
Check whether they run video or image ads and what language they target. A competitor running Spanish-only image ads, for example, is not a direct competitor in the US English market.

Evaluate their store and offer. The source rejects a competitor's store as 'completely trash' — minimal template, wrong product imagery — and notes a stronger brand presentation plus subscription option as a differentiator he could use.

Expect more competitors to appear over time; finding three already means the product is moving. Speed matters — a competitor found the same product 24 hours earlier, which the source treats as a meaningful head start.
caveats: Ad Library shows ads, not spend, so you cannot tell if a competitor's campaign is profitable.
Page Transparency and Ad Library interfaces change; verify current navigation in the tool.
New competitors with hours of runtime provide no validation either way.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Spy Crew as a budget alternative to full-price research tools
cards.summary: Use Spy Crew's bundled browser and tool access to get Kalodata, Shop Plus, PP Spy and other research utilities at a lower monthly cost than subscribing separately.
cards.use_when: Setting up a research stack when Kalodata's standalone price is the constraint.
steps: Recognize the cost problem the source is solving: Kalodata alone is $80/month.
Use Spy Crew's Pro plan at roughly $49/month, which the source says includes Kalodata access plus a customized browser environment.

Exploit the browser structure: every new tab opens Spy Crew's dashboard with a tool directory, including Runway ML, Tikstar, Playbook, Helium 10, Drop Spy, Future Live, cutout.pro, Shop Plus, Kalodata, PP Spy, Canva and PP Ads.
Use Shop Plus as a Kalodata 'dupe' for a second data angle, and PP Spy (Chrome extension) to check whether a competitor store has recently added new products.
Also keep free standalone tabs open for the core validation loop: Facebook Ad Library, Google Trends, Amazon, and Google search.
caveats: The source states he would not do product research the way he does without Spy Crew; this is a tool-access argument, not an endorsement of outcomes.
Tool bundles and pricing change — verify current plans and included tools before subscribing.
The video also contains promotional segments for the presenter's paid mentorship, which are not part of this method.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Searching for the most untapped products: sort and ignore images
cards.summary: In the product list, sort revenue lowest to highest and screen on graph shape first, using product images only to spot known-saturated items.
cards.use_when: Starting a live hunt in Kalodata and deciding which rows to click into.
steps: Filter down to one niche at a time rather than flooding the page with all categories. The source uses the last-30-days date range and only the products tab, ignoring the other top tabs.
Change the default sort from highest revenue to lowest revenue. The source's stated reason is that this surfaces the most untapped products.

On the list, ignore product images as a first screen. Don't even look at them — evaluate the graph shape, looking for a line that is not going down (flat or slightly uptrending is enough; it does not need to shoot to the moon).

Treat the image as a second, quick saturation check: if you recognize a long-established, heavily sold product (the source's example is moringa, seen multiple times in the same list and known to be widely run by friends and others on Facebook), skip it regardless of graph.
Use pattern recognition from daily hunting: seeing the same category repeatedly (e.g. GLP products everywhere on TikTok Shop) is itself a signal that a niche is hot.
caveats: The source admits he sometimes glances at the image anyway when the graph excites him; the primary screen remains the graph.
Niche familiarity is required for the image-based saturation check — beginners will not recognize long-running products.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Reading stacked hooks that introduce a novel ingredient or format
cards.summary: How branded ingredient or unusual format claims (liposomal, NAD, patches) create perceived sophistication and a reason to click.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a supplement or wellness product has a defensible angle beyond a commodity ingredient.
steps: Look at the label copy in the product image and product title for a branded or technical ingredient signal — the source points to 'liposomal' or 'NAD' as examples that sound sophisticated and differentiate a commodity.
Recognize that the ingredient itself does not need to be new; introducing a specific-sounding ingredient to the customer's mind as the solution is what the source says drives performance.

Check for format novelty within a known niche. The source maps six supplement formats — patches, consumables/pills, powders, liquids, resins, gummies — and treats a format not yet saturated in a hot niche as an opening; GLP patches were his example against abundant GLP pills and powders.
Combine ingredient/format novelty with the trend check: novelty explains why it is working now, Google Trends confirms the variation is still rising.
Reject pH products unless the company is introducing something new — a new angle or new ingredient — because the source knows how many pH products already exist.
caveats: 'Sophisticated-sounding ingredient' is a persuasion judgment, not a clinical claim; do not treat it as efficacy evidence.
Commodity supplements are a highly competitive niche in the source's view, even though they are the most profitable because they enable renewability.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Translating a TikTok-native creative into a Meta ad (mix-match)
cards.summary: Combine a validated short TikTok hook with a longer, more convincing creator body to produce a Meta-optimized ad.
cards.use_when: Building your first ad set after buying a validated product, especially when the top TikTok video is a very short viral clip.
steps: Take the validated short hook — the source's example is a 5-second clip opening with 'your insurance doesn't cover Zepbound, but GLP patches exist' — and use its first ~3 seconds as your hook.
Cut at roughly the 3-second mark into a longer creator video (the source uses a ~1 minute 10 second creator explaining her experience and answering comments) so the viewer gets depth and proof.

Apply the source's stated ad principles: lowest CPC and shortest/most fun videos are typically not the highest converters on Meta; the highest converters are the most convincing, and convincing takes time.
Use the TikTok-native short as the attention device and the Facebook-native long creator clip as the argument — the source notes the long clip would outperform the short one on Meta for that reason.
Do not simply rip one ad wholesale. The source warns that ripped ads make you indistinguishable from competitors — everyone can rip the same creative; editing your own is the differentiator.
Plan to make 5–8 ads when testing a product, per the source's testing practice.
caveats: The source's own scope note says to ignore instructions on editing mix-match creatives in this particular video; the concept appears here but is not developed as step-by-step editing instruction.
Hooks and clips should be validated by their own performance data, not copied blindly.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Acting on brand-new videos to get ahead of a spike
cards.summary: Use very recent video posting dates and rapid view velocity as an early-entry signal before a product saturates, and accept the gamble that comes with it.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to move immediately on a product whose graph is rising steeply and whose top videos were posted days ago.
steps: Check the posting date of the top video against today's date. In the source's example, a video posted June 5 had 8.39 million views by June 11 — six days — which he treats as an exceptional green flag.

Run rough arithmetic on recent units to estimate trajectory: a video posted four days earlier that already sold 45 units implies roughly 3,000 units/month if the pace holds, approaching the revenue of the current top video.

Interpret the timing advantage: getting in before the product is widely found lets you hold Facebook ad placements and bid ahead of later entrants, and the source says Meta favors advertisers with longer histories on a product (a 'legacy' advantage).
Verify the recency of multiple top videos, not just one — the source checks each and finds all were posted within days.

Accept the trade-off: a steeply rising product with no prior decline has no sustainability data. The source calls it a gamble — it can keep climbing or drop to zero and wipe out early advertisers along with everyone else.

Compare against established products that show a range of lows and highs over time (e.g. lows around a few hundred dollars/day with an overall uptrend), which the source calls a healthier signal even if less explosive.
caveats: The source states plainly that he cannot know whether the example product kept rising or collapsed by publication time.
Meta's favor toward earlier advertisers is presented as the source's belief, not a documented platform rule.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Pricing and offer strategy when translating a cheap TikTok product to Meta
cards.summary: Raise price and build an offer structure on your own store because Meta audiences respond to longer, more convincing ad-to-site experiences.
cards.use_when: You have validated a low-priced TikTok Shop product (e.g. $15) and need a viable offer for a Meta funnel.
steps: Accept that a $9.99 TikTok price is not a viable Meta price — the source rejects sub-$10 products because cheap impulse pricing leaves no margin for acquisition costs.

Reposition the product at a higher price on your own store. In the source's example, a $15 TikTok product could be sold around $29.99 with a buy-one-get-one-free offer, and shipping of $4–$5 can be charged.
Anchor the higher price to perceived value: the source argues people will pay more because Meta ads are longer and more convincing and the website looks better than a TikTok Shop listing.

Build in renewability where the product supports it — the source cites a subscription product generating over $5,000/month recurring, with a 33% subscription rate (1 in 3 customers), and describes that as the path to a durable brand.
Use a no-subscription high-volume product as a valid alternative: the source's own $1.5M store had zero subscribers.
caveats: The $29.99/BOGO and shipping numbers are the source's illustration, not a tested benchmark for every product.
A 33% subscription rate is one brand's reported result, not a promise.
The source notes supplements are highly competitive even though they are the most profitable because of renewability.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx

cards.title: Choosing a niche based on business model
cards.summary: Pick your research category according to whether you want recurring revenue or high-volume one-off sales.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to hunt in Kalodata's category filter before starting a product search.
steps: If you want MRR and subscription revenue, hunt in the health niche, because it lends itself to reusable products and subscription offers.

If you want high-volume, no-subscription ecommerce volume, the source points to beauty and personal care, women's wear and underwear, men's wear and underwear, home improvement, and jewelry and accessories.

Use the source's own contrast as the decision frame: his $1.5M store had no subscribers, while a separate product generated $5K/month recurring revenue with a 33% subscription rate — different models from the same system.
Filter one niche at a time in the tool rather than mixing categories on a single search, and only use the product tab plus the last-30-days range the source works with.
Treat category choice as a strategic decision made before you start hunting, not something to resolve by picking whatever appears on the first page.
caveats: The category list reflects the source's own experience, not a ranked study of niche profitability.
Supplements inside the health niche are noted as the most profitable but also very competitive.
cards.source_name: This Product Research Method Made Me $2.3M Dropshipping (LIVE HUNTING).docx
